Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq and his students: Abu Hanifa and Malik
hook: A gate of knowledge opened in Medina: Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq and the scholars who came to his circle.
scenes.0.text: He was born in Medina in the 80th or 83rd year of the Hijrah, i.e. 699 or 702. Most sources place his age at 83. His father is the Fifth Imam, Muhammad Bakr, and his lineage extends to Ali and Fatima. His mother is Umm Ferve, Qasim b. She's the daughter of Muhammad. Qasim is the grandson of Abu Bakr. In Shiite sources, he is the Sixth Imam. He is also mentioned in Sunni sources as a great scholar and a respected member of the Ahl al-Bayt. The people of Medina gave him this nickname because of his honesty and his confidence in the Assembly of Knowledge.

scenes.1.text: The youthful years of Kha'fer-i Saddiq coincided with a turbulent period when the Emevi dynasty began to dissolve. Soon, power passed into the hands of the Abbasids. During those years, there were many revolts and power struggles. But Hadhrat Sadiq did not participate in these uprisings. He devoted all his energies to learning, teaching and training students in Medina. He knew that protecting and spreading the Prophet's knowledge was a more permanent way than the sword. According to Shia sources, the Abbasid caliph **Mansur** became upset with her influence over the people and eventually poisoned her.

scenes.2.text: In Medina, around the Prophet's mosque, the lecture rings of the Prophet Ja'fer-i Sadiq were established. According to Shia sources, the number of people who listen to him reaches four thousand. Sheikh Mufid al-Irshad mentions four thousand in his work, while Ibn Ukde mentions four thousand in his book counting his disciples. Sheikh Tusi's Rical has about 3200 names. The numbers vary from source to source, but they all indicate that a very large learned society was established in Medina. People came to Medina from different cities, from different opinions, to listen to him.
scenes.2.art.actors.0.label: 1ytn1vq
Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq
scenes.3.text: The knowledge of Ja'fer-i-Sadik is especially mentioned in the fields of hadith, fiqh and kalam. This sect is called **the Jafari sect** because the Shia's fiqh is largely based on his and his father's traditions. According to Shiite sources, the knowledge of the imams is a trust passed down from father to son by the Prophet. He is also credited with works in chemistry and medicine, but these are not solid ratios. The algebra b. The rumor that he passed information to Hayyan is highly suspect. Much of the work in chemistry and alchemy may have been a product of later periods. His main legacy is the fiqh and hadith he teaches in class.
scenes.3.art.actors.0.label: 1ytn1vq
Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq
scenes.4.text: The relationship between Abu Hanifa, the founder of the Hanefi sect, and Ja'fer-i Sadiq is described as a scientific encounter between the two scholars. Sources say that the Prophet saw him both in Medina and in Iraq. It is said that Abu Hanifah consulted with the scholars of the Ahl al-Bayt and benefited from them, especially in the matter of akaid. In Sunni sources, the lineage of Abu Hanf's teachers is Hammâd b. And Abraham went up to the lowest place and the lowest place. Shi'a sources refer to Abu Hanifa as a disciple of Ja'fer-i Sadik. The Sunni narrative sees this relationship as a sign of respect, while the Shiite narrative sees it as a requirement.

scenes.5.text: According to Shi'a sources, Abu Hanf learnt from Ja'fer-i Sadik for two years and, describing these years, said: "Had it not been for those two years, Nu'man would have perished". Nu'man is the proper name of Abu Hanifa. It is disputed how old this saying is and whether it really belongs to Abu Hanifa. Some people put the blame on another teacher. The Ja'far reading places these two years in the ring of Hazrat Ja'fer-i-Saddik. It is also debatable which fiqh text belongs to him. But all this debate doesn't change the size and clarity of that ring in Medina.

scenes.6.text: **Malik b. Enes**, the founder of the Maliki sect and the great scholar of Medina, is mentioned among those who listened to the hadith of the Prophet Ja'fer-i Sadik. In Sheikh Saduk's work al-Hisal, it is reported that Malik went to the imam and listened to his hadith. In some Sunni books, however, this relationship is not mentioned. But not being in a book doesn't erase that ring that everyone knows in Medina. Malik, as one of the scholars of Medina, was among those who benefited from the council of the Imam of the Ahl al-Bayt, who taught in the same city.

scenes.7.text: Many Sunni scholars have also praised Ja'fer-i Sadik. Zeheb considers him one of the great scholars. His narratives are also found in the six most trusted Sunni hadith books, the Qutub-i-Sitte. The reason Buhari doesn't take revenge on him in Sahih is not because he sees him as weak. The main reason is that there are people who entered his council and attributed false hadiths to him. So it's not about the imam himself, it's about those who lie in his name. His nickname, "es-Sadik", which means "truthful", reminds us of his honesty in the face of such lies.
scenes.7.art.actors.0.label: 1ytn1vq

scenes.8.text: He died in Medina in the year 765 of the Hijrah, and was buried beside his father and grandfather in Jannatul-Baqi. In Shia sources, he is mentioned as the founder of the Ehl-i Beyt school and the Caferî sect. The circle of knowledge he built has been the cornerstone of this school. In Sunni sources, it is also one of the most respected links of Medina science. Thus, Shiite and Sunni traditions meet at the door of the Sadeq. The door of knowledge he opened in Medina never closed for centuries.

sunni.0.says: Born 80/83, died 148 H, Medina. His mother Umm Farwa (daughter of Qasim b. Muhammad). Malik heard hadith from him, and he had scholarly debates with Abu Hanifa. His reports are in the Kutub al-Sitta, not in Bukhari's Sahih. The attribution of chemistry is highly doubtful.

disputes.0.title: wi5w1j
Was Abu Hanifa a student of Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq?
disputes.0.shia: The scholarly relationship between Abu Hanifa and Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq is mentioned in both sources. In the Shia account Abu Hanifa is his student; Ibn Abi al-Hadid also counts him as a student. An early source for the "two years" saying has not been found.
disputes.0.sunni: The scholarly relationship between Abu Hanifa and Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq is mentioned in both sources. TDV writes this as meeting and benefiting in creed, and does not describe him as a student; the "two years" saying is not in early sources.
disputes.1.title: 1ekxows
Did Malik narrate from Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq?
disputes.1.shia: That Malik heard hadith from Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq is mentioned in both sources. In the Shia transmission, this rests on the report of going to him in al-Saduq's al-Khisal.
disputes.1.sunni: It is mentioned in both sources where Malik heard a hadith from Kha'fer-i-Saddik. TDV makes that clear.
disputes.2.title: 14qgmss
Does the knowledge of chemistry and medicine belong to Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq?
disputes.2.shia: The attribution of some works to Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq is disputed on both sides. In later Shia-Batini circles certain books are tied to him; some works of Jabir b. Hayyan present themselves as an exposition of his teaching.
disputes.2.sunni: The attribution of some works to Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq is disputed on both sides. TDV considers the report that he passed knowledge to Jabir highly doubtful; Ruska and Kraus find it baseless. Only the medical work called Ihtilaj al-a'da' is attributed to him.
questions.0: TDV attributes the absence of reports from Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq in Bukhari's Sahih not to weakness but to fabricated hadith having been ascribed to his name. Why does it become harder to protect a name within a wide circle of learning?
questions.1: The figure of four thousand occurs in al-Mufid and Ibn Uqda, and about 3,200 in al-Tusi. How do large numbers of narrators let one read the breadth of a circle of learning?
questions.2: The "two years" saying cannot be found in early sources. Why does a saying's being famous not by itself show its historical record?
questions.3: When the Umayyads were dissolved and the Abbasids ascended the throne, Ja'fer-i Saddiq did not rebel. Why do you think Ca'fer-i Sadik chose to teach instead of rebel?
questions.4: Malik and Hazrat Ja'fer-i Sadiq were raised in the same Medina. Why do you think common teachers and common myths explain the closeness between sects?
summary: He is the author of the book of Judges. 148 H) established a circle of open knowledge in Medina. It's also in the T.D.V. where Malik heard a hadith from him. His relationship with Abu Hanifa is mentioned in Shia sources as a student, in TDV as a scholarly discussion. The Jaffari sect was formed by the legends of this ring.
key: Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq and the school of learning
notes.0: Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq was born in Medina in 83 H (702) and died there in 148 H (765).
notes.1: He did not take part in political uprisings; he turned to knowledge.
notes.2: The number of students is given as roughly between 3200 and 4000, depending on the source.
notes.3: Ja'fari jurisprudence is known by his name.
notes.4: That Malik heard hadith from him is in TDV; his relationship with Abu Hanifa is disputed.
sunni.6.says: It is said that the Prophet died of poisoning in the year 148 AD.
